Zeus and Europa

Zeus transformed himself into a gentle white bull and mingled with the herd of Europa, a Phoenician princess. When she climbed onto his back, he leapt into the sea and swam to Crete, where she bore him Minos, Rhadamanthus and Sarpedon. The bull was placed among the stars as a reward.

Older roots

The constellation is one of the oldest recorded, appearing on the Sumerian 'Bull of Heaven' tablets and in Babylonian star catalogues over 3,000 years ago.

Castor and Pollux

Castor was the mortal son of Tyndareus and Pollux the immortal son of Zeus. When Castor was killed in battle, the grieving Pollux asked Zeus to let him share his immortality with his brother. Zeus placed them both in the sky as the Twins, and they became patrons of sailors and hospitality.

The crab of Lerna

While Heracles fought the many-headed Hydra, Hera sent a giant crab to pinch his heel and hinder him. Heracles crushed it, and Hera rewarded its loyalty by placing it in the sky. Though the crab played a minor role, its constellation sits between Leo and Gemini along the ecliptic.

Older associations

Ancient Egyptians and Babylonians linked this region to the scarab beetle and to a gateway of souls descending through the sky.

The Nemean Lion

The lion terrorised the region of Nemea and could not be wounded by any weapon. Heracles trapped it in a cave and strangled it with his bare hands, then wore its hide as armour. Zeus placed the lion in the sky to commemorate the feat, which became the first of the twelve labours.

Older roots

Mesopotamian records identify a lion constellation in this same region as early as 4000 BC, and the star Regulus was associated with kingship in both Babylonian and Persian tradition.

Astraea and the Golden Age

During the Golden Age, the goddess of justice lived among mortals. As humanity grew corrupt through the Silver and Bronze Ages, she withdrew to the mountains, and finally to the sky, where she became the constellation Virgo. Her scales were placed nearby as Libra.

Other identifications

Virgo has also been linked to Demeter, goddess of the harvest, and to Ishtar in Babylonian tradition, where Spica represented the ear of grain she carried.

Deep-sky objects

mythologyDetailed:
Scales of Astraea

Libra was originally part of Scorpius, forming the scorpion's claws. The Romans were the first to separate it into its own constellation, associating it with the scales of justice held by Astraea. When she fled the corrupt earth and was placed in the sky as Virgo, her scales were set beside her as Libra.

Babylonian origins

Babylonian astronomers called this region 'ZIB.BA.AN.NA' — the balance of heaven — and linked it to the autumn equinox, which occurred here roughly 2,000 years ago before precession shifted it into Virgo.

Libra contains few bright deep-sky objects. Gliese 581, a red dwarf about 20 light-years away, was once thought to host potentially habitable planets. NGC 5897 is a globular cluster visible in small telescopes.

The scorpion and Orion

Orion boasted that he could kill every animal on earth, so Gaia sent a giant scorpion to humble him. The scorpion stung Orion fatally, and Zeus placed both in the sky. They were set at opposite ends of the heavens — as Scorpius rises in the east, Orion sets in the west — so the hunter can never be stung again.

Babylonian roots

Babylonian star catalogues list a scorpion figure in this region as early as 1100 BC, one of the oldest recorded constellations.

Crotus and Chiron

Sagittarius is commonly linked to Crotus, son of Pan and Eupheme, who invented the bow and was placed among the stars by the Muses. An alternative tradition identifies the archer with Chiron, the wise centaur who taught Achilles and Heracles. The constellation is often drawn aiming its arrow at the heart of Scorpius, the scorpion.

Babylonian astronomers recorded a centaur-archer figure in this region as early as the 11th century BC, associated with the god Pabilsag.

When the monster Typhon stormed Olympus, the gods fled in disguise. Pan jumped into the Nile, and the part of him above water became a goat while the submerged half became a fish. Ganymede

Ganymede was the son of King Tros of Troy and was renowned for his beauty. Zeus, in the form of an eagle, carried him up to Olympus, where he replaced Hebe as cupbearer to the gods and was granted immortality. His pouring of nectar became the constellation Aquarius.

Older roots

Babylonian astronomers associated this region with their god Ea, who poured the waters of life from a great urn, and the Greeks inherited the imagery of a celestial water-pourer.

Asclepius and the serpent

Asclepius was the son of Apollo and a mortal woman, trained in medicine by the centaur Chiron. When he saw a serpent revive another with a herb, he learned to bring the dead back to life. Hades complained to Zeus that this upset the order of things, and Zeus struck Asclepius down with a thunderbolt. In honour of his skill, he was placed in the sky holding the serpent, and his staff — the Rod of Asclepius — remains a symbol of medicine today.

The 13th zodiac

Because the ecliptic passes through Ophiuchus, the Sun spends about 18 days in the constellation each year. Babylonian and later astronomers acknowledged this, but the twelve-sign zodiac was kept for convenience of twelve equal 30-degree divisions.

The hunter Orion

Orion was a giant huntsman, son of Poseidon, who could walk on water and boasted he could kill every beast on earth. Gaia sent a scorpion to humble him, and the sting killed him. Zeus placed him in the sky alongside the scorpion, at opposite ends of the heavens so they never share the night sky.

Older roots

The constellation is one of the oldest recorded. A carved mammoth tusk from roughly 32,000 BC shows a figure resembling Orion's Belt, and the stars appear in Babylonian star catalogues as 'The Heavenly Shepherd' as early as 1300 BC.

Callisto and Arcas

Callisto was a nymph and companion of Artemis who caught the eye of Zeus. When Hera discovered the affair, she transformed Callisto into a bear. Years later, her son Arcas, out hunting, nearly killed the bear before Zeus intervened, turning both mother and son into constellations — Ursa Major and Ursa Minor. Hera, still angry, persuaded Poseidon to keep them from ever dipping into the sea.

Many traditions

The seven stars of the Dipper have been named across cultures: the Bear in Greece, the Seven Sages in India, the Wagon in China, and the Great Bear's Tail among the Iroquois. In Norse tradition, they were seen as a wagon or plough.

Cassiopeia was the wife of King Cepheus of Aethiopia and mother of Andromeda. Her boast that she surpassed the sea-nymphs in beauty so enraged Poseidon that he sent a sea monster, Cetus, to ravage the coast. Cassiopeia was placed in the sky as punishment, and the constellation circles the celestial pole, spending half of every night hanging upside down as an eternal humiliation.

One tradition identifies Cygnus with the swan Zeus became to approach Leda, mother of Helen of Troy and the Dioscuri. A third tradition links the constellation to Orpheus, the legendary musician, who after his death was transformed into a swan and placed beside his lyre (the constellation Lyra) in the sky.

After his wife Eurydice died, he descended to the underworld to bring her back, but lost her when he looked behind him too soon. Later killed by the Maenads, his lyre was placed in the sky by the Muses, alongside his memory as the constellation.

Orion's hound

Canis Major represents one of the two dogs accompanying Orion the Hunter, along with Canis Minor. The ancient Greeks and Romans noted that Sirius rose with the Sun during the hottest weeks of summer — the 'dog days' — which they believed brought fever and drought.

An oracle declared that only the sacrifice of Andromeda could appease the god, so she was chained to a rock by the sea. Perseus, flying past on his winged sandals, saw her, killed the monster, and married her. All the figures — Cassiopeia, Cepheus, Andromeda, Perseus and Cetus — are placed together in the sky.

When Bellerophon tried to fly to Mount Olympus, Zeus sent a gadfly to unseat him, and Pegasus continued alone to the home of the gods, where he carried Zeus's thunderbolts. Ariadne was the daughter of King Minos of Crete, who helped Theseus escape the labyrinth by giving him a ball of thread. Cepheus was the king of Aethiopia, married to the beautiful but boastful Cassiopeia. Auriga is commonly identified with Erichthonius, son of Hephaestus and Gaia, who was raised by Athena and became king of Athens. Unlike the other centaurs, who were wild and violent, Chiron was wise, kind and skilled in medicine, music and prophecy. The king's dogs

A queen's sacrifice

Berenice II, queen of Ptolemaic Egypt, vowed to cut off her long hair and dedicate it to Aphrodite if her husband Ptolemy III returned safely from war. He did, and she kept her promise. The hair disappeared from the temple, and the court astronomer Conon of Samos declared that Aphrodite had placed it among the stars. The Greek poet Callimachus wrote a famous poem about the lock, which survives in a Latin translation by Catullus. The constellation is one of the few in the sky named for a real historical person.

Phaethon, son of Helios the Sun, begged to drive his father's chariot across the sky for a day. The bird of fire

Phoenix the constellation was introduced in 1598 by Petrus Plancius, and takes its name from the legendary phoenix — a bird that lives for centuries, dies in flames, and is reborn from its own ashes. The toucan is a bird native to the tropical forests of Central and South America, unknown to the ancient Greeks and Romans — so unlike the classical constellations, Tucana is a modern addition to the sky, unconnected to any mythological tradition.

Scutum was introduced by Johannes Hevelius in 1687 as 'Scutum Sobiescianum' — the Shield of Sobieski — in honour of King John III Sobieski of Poland, whose cavalry charge at the Battle of Vienna in 1683 had turned back the Ottoman army. deepSkyObjects:
Deep-sky objects

Serpens contains the Eagle Nebula (M16) with its iconic Pillars of Creation, imaged by Hubble in 1995. It also contains the globular cluster M5, the open cluster M16, and the faint planetary nebula NGC 6537 — the Red Spider Nebula. The constellation lies along the Milky Way and is rich in star-forming regions.

Its stars are dim — none brighter than magnitude 4.5 — but the constellation lies away from the Milky Way and contains a rich field of distant galaxies. It is unrelated to the Sextant constellation 'Sextans Uraniae', which Hevelius also proposed but was never accepted.

mythologySummary: Sextans has no ancient mythology. It was created by Hevelius in 1687 and named after the sextant he used to measure star positions, in memory of the instrument destroyed in the fire that consumed his observatory.
mythologyDetailed:
The sextant of Hevelius

Sextans was introduced by Johannes Hevelius in his 1687 star atlas, drawn as the sextant he had used for decades to catalogue the positions of stars. In 1679 his observatory in Danzig was destroyed by fire, and the sextant with it. Hevelius commemorated the instrument by placing it in the sky as a constellation. It was the last of the classical instrument constellations to be added, and it remains one of the faintest — a quiet memorial to a lifetime of observation.

Deep-sky objects

Sextans is rich in faint galaxies, including the Spindle Galaxy (NGC 3115), a bright lenticular galaxy, and the Sextans Dwarf spheroidal galaxy — a very faint satellite of the Milky Way discovered in 1990. The constellation also contains several galaxy groups accessible to moderate telescopes.
